title: Visualisation
body:
We have used several different types of plot in this book, created using the Plot module from the separate owl-plplot package. It is designed to make reasonably complex plots with minimal coding effort, and is built on PLplot1 but hides much of its complexity. PLplot calls the underlying graphics device driver to render the plot. Code for several of the figures in this book has already been included; in this appendix we will use many other examples to demonstrate how to draw various typical plots in OCaml.

Running the examples

Source: code/chapB_visualisation
Run: python3 scripts/run_chapterB.py --output /tmp/chapterB

The container includes owl-plplot and the PLplot Cairo driver. The command regenerates the figures. For interactive use, load this setup in utop:

OCAML
#require "owl";;
#require "owl-plplot";;
open Owl;;
open Owl_plplot;;
Owl_stats_prng.init 102;;
#mod_use "/opt/book/code/chapB_visualisation/book_visualisation.ml";;

B.1 Plotting in Owl

B.1.1 Create Plots

Let’s start with the standard way to create a plot using Plot.create. Here is its current type, inspected from Owl_plplot.Plot:

OCAML SESSION
val create : ?m:int -> ?n:int -> string -> Owl_plplot.Plot.handle

For example,

OCAML
let example_02 () =
  let f x = Maths.sin x /. x in
    let h = Plot.create "plot_001.png" in

    Plot.set_title h "Function: f(x) = sine x / x";
    Plot.set_xlabel h "x-axis";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "y-axis";
    Plot.set_font_size h 8.;
    Plot.set_pen_size h 3.;
    Plot.plot_fun ~h f 1. 15.;
    Plot.output h;;
example_02 ();;

In these examples, we obtain a handle h from the create function. The file-name suffix selects the PLplot output device, which must be available in the environment. In this case, we want to create a PNG image that plots sin⁡(x)∕x on [1,15] so we will use the plot_fun function. We also set the x- and y-axis labels and figure title, together with the font size and line width. You will find that these commands are similar to those in other plotting tools such as Matplotlib. Calling Plot.output h renders the accumulated drawing operations and closes the PLplot output. This is the final step in each example. The generated figure is shown below.

B.1.2 Specification

For most high-level plotting functions in Owl, there is an optional parameter, spec. This takes a list of specifications to exercise fine control over the plot’s appearance. Each plotting function uses a different subset of the spec options; options that it does not use are ignored. For value-bearing options such as RGB and LineStyle, the last occurrence takes effect when the same option is repeated.

In the following, we will provide some examples using the spec parameter to fine tune Owl’s plots. The first example in Fig. B.2 shows how to configure the mesh plot using ZLine, Contour, and other spec parameters.

OCAML
let example_03 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-2.5) 2.5 (-2.5) 2.5 50 50 in
    let z = Mat.(sin ((x * x) + (y * y))) in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:3 "plot_020.png" in

    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine XY ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine X ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 0 2;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine Y ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine Y; NoMagColor ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine Y; Contour ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 2;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ ZLine XY; Curtain ] x y z);

    Plot.output h;;
example_03 ();;

The second example in Fig. B.3 shows how to tune the surf plotting function when drawing a 3D surface.

OCAML
let example_04 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-1.) 1. (-1.) 1. 50 50 in
    let z = Mat.(tanh ((x * x) + (y * y))) in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:3 "plot_021.png" in

    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ Faceted ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 0 2;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ NoMagColor ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ Contour ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ Curtain ] x y z);

    Plot.subplot h 1 2;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ Altitude 10.; Azimuth 125. ] x y z);

    Plot.output h;;
example_04 ();;

B.1.3 Subplots

You might have already spotted another feature in the previous example: subplots. You can change the number of rows and columns of the subplot layout by varying the values of the m and n parameters in the create function. Select a subplot with Plot.subplot h i j, where i and j are zero-based row and column indices.

OCAML
let example_05 () =
  let f p i = match i with
      | 0 -> Stats.gaussian_rvs ~mu:0. ~sigma:0.5 +. p.(1)
      | _ -> Stats.gaussian_rvs ~mu:0. ~sigma:0.1 *. p.(0)
    in
    let y = Stats.gibbs_sampling f [|0.1;0.1|] 5_000
      |> Mat.of_arrays in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:2 "plot_002.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;

    (* subplot at 0,0 *)
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.set_title h "Bivariate model";
    Plot.scatter ~h (Mat.col y 0) (Mat.col y 1);

    (* subplot at 0,1 *)
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.set_title h "Distribution of y";
    Plot.set_xlabel h "y";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Frequency";
    Plot.histogram ~h ~bin:50 (Mat.col y 1);

    (* subplot at 1,0 *)
    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.set_title h "Distribution of x";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Frequency";
    Plot.histogram ~h ~bin:50 (Mat.col y 0);

    (* subplot at 1,1 *)
    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.set_foreground_color h 255 0 0;
    Plot.set_title h "Sine function";
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 2 ] Maths.sin 0. 28.);
    Plot.autocorr ~h (Mat.sequential 1 28);

    Plot.output h;;
example_05 ();;

B.1.4 Multiple Lines

You can certainly plot multiple functions in the same plot. Fig. B.5a is an example with both sine and cosine lines in one plot.

OCAML
let example_06 () =
  let h = Plot.create "plot_024.png" in
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,0,255); Marker "#[0x2299]";
      MarkerSize 8. ] Maths.sin 0. 9.);
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ RGB (255,0,0); Marker "#[0x0394]";
      MarkerSize 8. ] Maths.cos 0. 9.);
    Plot.legend_on h [|"Sine function"; "Cosine function"|];
    Plot.output h;;
example_06 ();;

Fig. B.5b is another example showing both the histogram and line plots in one figure. The histogram shows counts; the overlaid Gaussian density is multiplied by 100. An approximate count-scale overlay would instead multiply the density by the sample size and bin width.

OCAML
let example_07 () =
  (* generate data *)
    let g x = (Stats.gaussian_pdf x ~mu:0. ~sigma:1.) *. 100. in
    let y = Mat.gaussian ~mu:0. ~sigma:1. 1 1000 in

    (* plot multiple data sets *)
    let h = Plot.create "plot_025.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;
    Plot.(histogram ~h ~spec:[ RGB (255,0,50) ] ~bin:100 y);
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,0,255); LineWidth 2. ]
      g (-4.) 4.);
    Plot.legend_on h [|"data"; "model"|];

    Plot.output h;;
example_07 ();;

So, by passing the same handle with ~h to successive plotting calls before Plot.output h, you can add datasets to the same figure.

B.1.5 Legend

The plot legend can be turned on and off by calling Plot.legend_on and Plot.legend_off respectively. When you call Plot.legend_on, you must provide an array of legend names in the order of the plotted datasets. The position is optional and defaults to NorthEast. There are eight named positions in Plot:

OCAML SESSION
type legend_position =
  Owl_plplot.Plot.legend_position =
    North
  | South
  | West
  | East
  | NorthWest
  | NorthEast
  | SouthWest
  | SouthEast

The following example shows how to control the legend, and the resulting figure is shown in Fig. B.6a.

OCAML
let example_09 () =
  (* generate data *)
    let x = Mat.(uniform 1 20 *$ 10.) in
    let y = Mat.(uniform 1 20) in
    let z = Mat.gaussian 1 20 in

    (* plot multiple data sets *)
    let h = Plot.create "plot_026.png" in
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,0,255); LineStyle 1;
      Marker "*" ] Maths.sin 1. 8.);
    Plot.(plot_fun ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,255,0); LineStyle 2;
      Marker "+" ] Maths.cos 1. 8.);
    Plot.scatter ~h x y;
    Plot.stem ~h x z;

    let u = Mat.(abs(gaussian 1 10 *$ 0.3)) in
    Plot.(bar ~h ~spec:[ RGB (255,255,0); FillPattern 3 ] u);

    let v = Mat.(neg u *$ 0.3) in
    let u = Mat.sequential 1 10 in
    Plot.(area ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,255,0); FillPattern 4 ] u v);

    (* set up legend *)
    Plot.(legend_on h ~position:NorthEast
      [|"test 1"; "test 2"; "scatter"; "stem"; "bar"; "area"|]);
    Plot.output h;;
example_09 ();;

B.1.6 Drawing Patterns

The plotting module supports multiple line patterns. Fig. B.6b demonstrates them.

OCAML
let example_10 () =
  let h = Plot.create "plot_004.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;
    Plot.set_pen_size h 2.;
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 1 ] 1. 1. 9. 1.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 2 ] 1. 2. 9. 2.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 3 ] 1. 3. 9. 3.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 4 ] 1. 4. 9. 4.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 5 ] 1. 5. 9. 5.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 6 ] 1. 6. 9. 6.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 7 ] 1. 7. 9. 7.);
    Plot.(draw_line ~h ~spec:[ LineStyle 8 ] 1. 8. 9. 8.);
    Plot.set_xrange h 0. 10.;
    Plot.set_yrange h 0. 9.;
    Plot.output h;;
example_10 ();;

Similarly, we can also fill rectangles with different patterns, as shown in Fig. B.7a.

OCAML
let example_11 () =
  let h = Plot.create "plot_005.png" in
    Array.init 9 (fun i ->
      let x0, y0 = 0.5, float_of_int i +. 1.0 in
      let x1, y1 = 4.5, float_of_int i +. 0.5 in
      Plot.(draw_rect ~h ~spec:[ FillPattern i ] x0 y0 x1 y1);
      Plot.(text ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,255,0) ] 2.3 (y0-.0.2)
        ("pattern: " ^ (string_of_int i)))
    ) |> ignore;

    Plot.output h;;
example_11 ();;

B.2 Plot Types

Having introduced these plotting elements, we will now demonstrate some of the different supported plot types.

Line plot (Fig. B.7b) is the most basic type. You can specify the colour, marker, and line style in the function.

OCAML
let example_12 () =
  let x = Mat.linspace 0. 2. 100 in
    let y0 = Mat.sigmoid x in
    let y1 = Mat.map Maths.sin x in
    let h = Plot.create "plot_022.png" in
    Plot.(plot ~h ~spec:[ RGB (255,0,0); LineStyle 1;
      Marker "#[0x2299]"; MarkerSize 8. ] x y0);
    Plot.(plot ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,255,0); LineStyle 2;
      Marker "#[0x0394]"; MarkerSize 8. ] x y1);
    Plot.(legend_on h ~position:SouthEast [|"sigmoid"; "sine"|]);
    Plot.output h;;
example_12 ();;

Next is the Scatter Plot. As with the line plot, you can specify the marker type and marker size. The example below in Fig. B.8 shows various marker shapes, specified using PLplot escape strings containing hexadecimal Unicode code points.

OCAML
let example_13 () =
  let x = Mat.uniform 1 30 in
    let y = Mat.uniform 1 30 in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:3 ~n:3 "plot_006.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2295]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x229a]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 0 2;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2206]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x229e]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2217]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 1 2;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2296]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 2 0;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2666]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 2 1;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x22a1]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 2 2;
    Plot.(scatter ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x22b9]";
      MarkerSize 5. ] x y);
    Plot.output h;;
example_13 ();;

The Stairs plot, or stairstep plot, draws the supplied x and y values as a staircase-like curve (Fig. B.9).

OCAML
let example_14 () =
  let x = Mat.linspace 0. 6.5 20 in
    let y = Mat.map Maths.sin x in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_007.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.plot_fun ~h Maths.sin 0. 6.5;
    Plot.(stairs ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,128,255) ] x y);
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(plot ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,0,0) ] x y);
    Plot.(stairs ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,128,255) ] x y);
    Plot.output h;;
example_14 ();;

The box plot on the right of Fig. B.10 shows datasets in terms of their quartiles and is often used in descriptive statistics. Here each row of y2 supplies one box: the box spans the first and third quartiles, the line marks the median, and the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum. The left panel is a bar plot of y1.

OCAML
let example_15 () =
  let y1 = Mat.uniform 1 10 in
    let y2 = Mat.uniform 10 100 in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_008.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(bar ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,153,51); FillPattern 3 ] y1);
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(boxplot ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,153,51) ] y2);
    Plot.output h;;
example_15 ();;

Fig. B.11 shows a stem plot.

OCAML
let example_16 () =
  let x = Mat.linspace 0.5 2.5 25 in
    let y = Mat.map (Stats.exponential_pdf ~lambda:0.1) x in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_009.png" in
    Plot.set_background_color h 255 255 255;
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.set_foreground_color h 0 0 0;
    Plot.stem ~h x y;
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(stem ~h ~spec:[ Marker "#[0x2295]";
      MarkerSize 5.; LineStyle 1 ] x y);
    Plot.output h;;
example_16 ();;

As stem plots are often used to show sample autocorrelation at different lags, the Plot module includes the autocorr function for your convenience. Fig. B.12 shows examples for sampled sine values and uniform random values.

OCAML
let example_17 () =
  let x = Mat.linspace 0. 8. 30 in
    let y0 = Mat.map Maths.sin x in
    let y1 = Mat.uniform 1 30 in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_010.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.set_title h "Sine";
    Plot.autocorr ~h y0;
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.set_title h "Uniform";
    Plot.autocorr ~h y1;
    Plot.output h;;
example_17 ();;

The Area Plot is similar to a line plot except that it fills the space between the line and the x-axis (Fig. B.13).

OCAML
let example_18 () =
  let x = Mat.linspace 0. 8. 100 in
    let y = Mat.map Maths.atan x in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_011.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(area ~h ~spec:[ FillPattern 1 ] x y);
    let x = Mat.linspace 0. (2. *. 3.1416) 100 in
    let y = Mat.map Maths.sin x in
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(area ~h ~spec:[ FillPattern 2 ] x y);
    Plot.output h;;
example_18 ();;

The Histogram Plot and CDF Plot are very commonly used when visualising a series of measurements. You can easily plot the histogram and empirical cumulative distribution of the data using the histogram and ecdf functions. Fig. B.14 shows two examples.

OCAML
let example_19 () =
  let x = Mat.gaussian 200 1 in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:2 "plot_012.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.set_title h "histogram";
    Plot.histogram ~h ~bin:25 x;
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.set_title h "empirical cdf";
    Plot.ecdf ~h x;
    Plot.output h;;
example_19 ();;

In Owl, it is straightforward to use a logarithmic scale on either or both of the x- and y-axes, as the code below and Fig. B.15 show. Values on a logarithmic axis must be positive. If x is omitted, these functions use indices starting at 1; thus the right-hand panels plot against sample indices rather than the supplied x values.

OCAML
let example_20 () =
  let x = Mat.logspace (-1.5) 2. 50 in
    let y = Mat.map Maths.exp x in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:2 "plot_013.png" in

    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.set_xlabel h "Input Data X";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Input Data Y";
    Plot.(loglog ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,255,0); LineStyle 2;
      Marker "+" ] ~x:x y);

    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.set_xlabel h "Index of Input Data Y";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Input Data Y";
    Plot.(loglog ~h ~spec:[ RGB (0,0,255); LineStyle 1;
      Marker "*" ] y);

    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.set_xlabel h "Input Data X";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Input Data Y";
    Plot.semilogx ~h ~x:x y;

    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.set_xlabel h "Index of Input Data Y";
    Plot.set_ylabel h "Input Data Y";
    Plot.semilogy ~h y;

    Plot.output h;;
example_20 ();;

We have already shown some examples of 3D plots earlier. Four functions in the Plot module visualise values on an x–y grid: surf and mesh draw 3D surfaces, while heatmap and contour show the values in two dimensions using colour and contour lines, respectively. We look first at the mesh and surf functions (Fig. B.16).

OCAML
let example_21 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-2.5) 2.5 (-2.5) 2.5 100 100 in
    let z0 = Mat.(sin ((x **$ 2.) + (y **$ 2.))) in
    let z1 = Mat.(cos ((x **$ 2.) + (y **$ 2.))) in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:2 "plot_014.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.surf ~h x y z0;
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.mesh ~h x y z0;
    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.surf ~h x y z1;
    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.mesh ~h x y z1;
    Plot.output h;;
example_21 ();;

You can control the viewpoint with the Altitude and Azimuth options in spec, both measured in degrees. The code below shows an example (Fig. B.17).

OCAML
let example_22 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-2.5) 2.5 (-2.5) 2.5 100 100 in
    let z = Mat.(sin ((x * x) + (y * y))) in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:1 ~n:3 "plot_015.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Altitude 50.; Azimuth 120. ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Altitude 65.; Azimuth 120. ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 0 2;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Altitude 80.; Azimuth 120. ] x y z);
    Plot.output h;;
example_22 ();;

Fig. B.18 shows a second example, displaying one surface with different plotting options.

OCAML
let example_23 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-3.) 3. (-3.) 3. 50 50 in
    let z = Mat.(
      3. $* ((1. $- x) **$ 2.) * exp (neg (x **$ 2.) -
      ((y +$ 1.) **$ 2.)) - (10. $* (x /$ 5. -
      (x **$ 3.) - (y **$ 5.)) * (exp (neg (x **$ 2.) -
      (y **$ 2.)))) - ((1./.3.) $* exp (neg ((x +$ 1.) **$ 2.) -
      (y **$ 2.))))
    in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:3 "plot_016.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.surf ~h x y z;
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.mesh ~h x y z;
    Plot.subplot h 0 2;
    Plot.(surf ~h ~spec:[ Contour ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Contour; Azimuth 115.;
      NoMagColor ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Azimuth 115.; ZLine X;
      NoMagColor; RGB (61,129,255) ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 1 2;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Azimuth 115.; ZLine Y;
      NoMagColor; RGB (130,255,40) ] x y z);
    Plot.output h;;
example_23 ();;

Finally, let’s look at the heatmap and contour plot for the same mathematical function as in the preceding example. The generated figures are shown in Fig. B.19.

OCAML
let example_24 () =
  let x, y = Mat.meshgrid (-3.) 3. (-3.) 3. 100 100 in
    let z = Mat.(
      3. $* ((1. $- x) **$ 2.) * exp (neg (x **$ 2.) -
      ((y +$ 1.) **$ 2.)) - (10. $* (x /$ 5. - (x **$ 3.) -
      (y **$ 5.)) * (exp (neg (x **$ 2.) - (y **$ 2.)))) -
      ((1./.3.) $* exp (neg ((x +$ 1.) **$ 2.) - (y **$ 2.))))
    in
    let h = Plot.create ~m:2 ~n:2 "plot_017.png" in
    Plot.subplot h 0 0;
    Plot.(mesh ~h ~spec:[ Contour ] x y z);
    Plot.subplot h 0 1;
    Plot.heatmap ~h x y z;
    Plot.subplot h 1 0;
    Plot.mesh ~h x y z;
    Plot.subplot h 1 1;
    Plot.contour ~h x y z;
    Plot.output h;;
example_24 ();;

1PLplot library: https://plplot.sourceforge.net/
